title: A warm breeding season was followed by lower next-year counts in the warm part and higher counts in the cool part of 368 bird species ranges in North American surveys, 1970-2024
abstract: Question: does the relation between breeding-season warmth and bird counts depend on the position of a route in the thermal range of each species? Climate-niche theory predicts better results after a warm season in the cool part of a range and worse results in the warm part. Data: North American Breeding Bird Survey 2025 release (1970-2024; 6,870,825 route-species-year records; 368 species; 4,068 routes) and NOAA GHCN_CAMS May-July temperature. Method: thermal niche position (TNP) is the route 1971-2000 climate as a standard score in the abundance-weighted range of the species. We modelled log(count + 1) with species x route x observer and species x year fixed effects, the detrended anomaly of the previous and the same season, their TNP interactions, and survey-weather and date controls. Intervals are two-way clustered by spatial block and year. The plan was written before the fits. Result: the previous-season anomaly x TNP interaction was -0.42 (95% interval -0.57 to -0.27) in 100 x log-count units per 1 C per SD. The previous-season slope was +0.76 in the coolest TNP quintile and -0.57 in the warmest. The interaction was negative in all four East/West x 1970-1996/1997-2024 subsets (three intervals exclude zero), in the latitude part (-0.61) and the non-latitude part (-0.23) of TNP, and after a year-relabel permutation test. A placebo with the next-season anomaly gave +0.05 (-0.16 to 0.26). 63% of species had negative estimates. Limitations: no detection model, coarse 0.5 degree temperature, a range truncated by the survey network, a small effect of about 1% per C, and a correlational design. The year-to-year response does not prove a long-term trend response.
